The word anorak has two distinct meanings as a noun. Both are correct and widely used, but in very different contexts. You need to know both to fully understand this word.

An anorak is a waterproof or windproof jacket with a hood attached. Its most recognizable feature is that it is usually a pullover style — meaning you slide it over your head to wear it, instead of zipping or buttoning it up the front like a coat. It is typically thick, warm, and practical rather than stylish. Think of the kind of jacket a hiker, a mountaineer, or someone going out in cold, rainy, or windy weather would wear.

Anoraks are strongly associated with outdoor activities — hiking, skiing, camping, birdwatching, and similar pursuits. They prioritize function over fashion. The jacket often has a large front pocket (sometimes called a kangaroo pocket), drawstrings to tighten the hood, and is made from tough, weather-resistant material.

Example sentences:

  • "She pulled on her anorak before heading out into the rain."
  • "He always wore his old green anorak on camping trips."
Meaning 2: A Socially Awkward Enthusiast (British Slang)

This is where the word gets interesting. In British English, "anorak" is also used as a slang term to describe a person who has an obsessive, intense, and very detailed interest in a subject that most people find boring or overly technical.

The key qualities of an "anorak" in this sense are:

  • They know an extraordinary amount about their chosen topic — far more than anyone would normally consider necessary.
  • Their interest is often seen as nerdy, dry, or unfashionable by others.
  • They tend to be socially awkward or at least perceived that way.
  • They may talk about their interest endlessly, even when others aren't interested.

Classic examples of "anorak" hobbies or interests include:

  • Train spotting (memorizing train numbers, schedules, and engine types)
  • Amateur radio operation
  • Stamp collecting
  • Bus route memorization
  • Obsessive statistics about a sport
  • Model railway building

The term is usually mildly mocking or teasing, but it is not always deeply insulting. In many cases, it is used affectionately — almost like fondly poking fun at someone for their harmless but overly intense hobby. Among people who share the same obsessive interest, calling each other "anoraks" can even be a term of solidarity.

Example sentences:

  • "He's a complete anorak — he knows the departure times of every bus in the city."
  • "A group of train anoraks gathered on the platform with their notebooks."
  • "She admits she's a bit of an anorak when it comes to 1970s British television."

The slang meaning grew directly from the jacket meaning, and understanding this makes the word much easier to remember.

The stereotype in Britain was that certain hobbyists — particularly train spotters, who would stand on railway platforms for hours in all weather, writing down train numbers — wore practical, unglamorous anoraks. The jacket became strongly associated with this image of the obsessive, slightly awkward enthusiast. Over time, the jacket's name transferred to the person wearing it. So if someone calls you an anorak, they are essentially painting a picture of you as someone who would stand in the rain in a functional jacket, furiously scribbling notes about something most people don't care about.
Important Things to Know About Usage

1. The slang meaning is primarily British.
If you use "anorak" to mean an obsessive enthusiast, people in the UK will understand you immediately. However, in American English, this slang meaning is not widely known or used. Americans would typically say "nerd," "geek," or "obsessive" instead.

2. The jacket meaning is understood more broadly.
The jacket itself is known in many countries, though it may go by different names in different places (for example, "parka" is sometimes used similarly, though a parka is slightly different in style).

3. Context tells you which meaning is meant.

  • If someone says "I left my anorak at home and got soaked," they mean the jacket.
  • If someone says "He's such an anorak about Formula 1," they mean the enthusiast.
  • There is almost never any confusion because the sentences that use each meaning look completely different.

3. Tone depends on relationship and context.

  • Said by a stranger about someone else: mildly mocking.
  • Said among friends: affectionate and teasing.
  • Said by someone about themselves: self-deprecating humour, often with a smile.

Meaning 1A hooded, waterproof pullover jacket for outdoor use
Meaning 2(British slang) A person with an obsessive, nerdy interest in a dull or technical subject
Tone of Meaning 2Mildly mocking, but can be affectionate or self-deprecating
Where Meaning 2 is usedPrimarily Britain

The word "anorak" is a beautifully British piece of vocabulary — practical on the outside (it's just a jacket), but rich with cultural meaning the moment you use it to describe a person.
